tuning.title: Known mount issues & compensations
tuning.intro: Every mount has known mechanical quirks. Pick your model to see what typically limits it and the compensations — most of them free — that work around each one.

avx.name: Celestron Advanced VX (AVX)
avx.summary: Community-reported AVX behaviour: significant backlash — worst on the declination axis — plus sizeable periodic error in right ascension. Roughly 70% of the achievable improvement comes from free tuning, before buying anything.

dec_backlash.label: Declination backlash
dec_backlash.symptom: Guiding corrections in DEC take seconds to bite, overshoot, or ping-pong between north and south.
dec_backlash.why: The worm/gear coupling has play: every time a correction reverses direction, the motor must first cross the dead zone before the axis actually moves.

periodic_error.label: Periodic error (RA)
periodic_error.symptom: Stars trail east–west on unguided exposures; guiding shows a slow wave plus a fast ripple in RA.
periodic_error.why: The RA worm's machining error repeats every turn: a slow ~620 s component of about 15″ peak-to-peak (easy to correct) plus a fast ~11 s oscillation that guiding struggles to follow.

east_heavy.title: Balance deliberately east-heavy in RA
steps: Balance the mount normally, then offset the counterweight slightly so the east side is a touch heavier — the axis always pulls against the worm.
After a meridian flip, re-offset the load so it stays east-heavy.
Goal: keep the worm pressed against one flank of the gear, so RA backlash disappears from guiding.
Recommended by Celestron; users report 1.5–2.25″ RMS dropping to 0.85–1.25″ when combined with PEC and PHD2 backlash compensation.

dec_unidirectional.title: Guide declination in one direction only
steps: Bias the polar alignment very slightly (a few arc-minutes) so declination always drifts the same way.
In PHD2, set DEC guiding to “North only” or “South only”, matching the drift direction.
Corrections never reverse, so DEC backlash never engages — the classic AVX workaround.

guiding_assistant.title: Run PHD2's Guiding Assistant
steps: Run the Guiding Assistant (Tools menu) for a few minutes on a star near the meridian and the celestial equator.
It measures DEC backlash and seeing, then proposes backlash compensation and min-move settings.
Accept the suggestions, then verify over a few minutes of guiding. Free and essential (~15 min).

pec.title: Train PEC + Predictive PEC in RA
steps: Record PEC in the mount over at least one full worm cycle (~10 min): the slow ~620 s / ~15″ peak-to-peak component corrects well.
Enable PHD2's Predictive PEC (PPEC) algorithm in RA so the residual error is learned and anticipated.
The fast ~11 s oscillation is hard to guide out — smooth it with short guide exposures (0.5–1 s).

celestron-eq-generic.name: Celestron EQ (CGEM, CGX…)
celestron-eq-generic.summary: Celestron German equatorials share the AVX family traits in milder form: some worm backlash and moderate periodic error. Careful balance, measurement and guiding setup remove most of it for free.

backlash.label: Axis backlash
backlash.symptom: Corrections take a moment to engage after changing direction; the star wanders around centre.
backlash.why: All worm drives have some play; it grows with a loose worm mesh and shows most in declination, where corrections keep reversing.

periodic_error.label: Periodic error (RA)
periodic_error.symptom: Stars trail slowly east–west on unguided exposures, repeating over a few minutes.
periodic_error.why: The worm gear's machining tolerances repeat every worm turn; the error is periodic, so it can be measured and corrected.

balance.title: Balance both axes properly
steps: Balance DEC first (scope + all gear mounted), then RA with the counterweights.
Leave a slight east-heavy bias in RA so the worm stays loaded on one flank.
Re-check balance after every gear change or meridian flip.

cables.title: Route the cables
steps: Attach cables to the mount so nothing snags or pulls as it tracks.
Leave a service loop at the axes; a taut cable reads as sudden guide spikes.
Re-check with the scope pointed where you will actually image.

polar_quality.title: Nail the polar alignment
steps: Use the polar-scope tools above (or a plate-solving routine) and take your time.
Poor polar alignment becomes DEC drift the guider must constantly fight.
Re-check after any bump or tripod move.

backlash_measure.title: Measure the backlash
steps: Run PHD2's Guiding Assistant for a few minutes near the meridian and the celestial equator.
Apply the backlash compensation and min-move values it suggests.
Re-measure after any mechanical adjustment (worm mesh, balance).

altaz-generic.summary: An alt-az GoTo tracks well but the field rotates: long exposures smear at the edges. Keep subs short and make the star alignment impeccable; backlash matters less since tracking rarely reverses.

field_rotation.symptom: Stars at the frame edges trace arcs around the centre on longer exposures.

short_exposures.title: Keep exposures short
steps: Keep subs short (15–30 s) and stack many of them.
Avoid targets near the zenith, where rotation is fastest.
For longer subs, consider an equatorial wedge (turns the mount into an EQ).

careful_align.title: Careful 2–3 star alignment
steps: Center each alignment star precisely — use a reticle eyepiece, or defocus slightly to judge centring.
Pick well-spread stars (the sequence above already does).
Redo the alignment after any bump or power cycle.

balance.title: Balance the tube
steps: Balance the tube fore/aft with all gear mounted so the drives are not fighting gravity.
Keep the load within the mount's rating — alt-az drives stall gracelessly.
Re-check after adding a camera or heavier eyepiece.

tutorial.title: How to set up and use your polar scope
tutorial.intro: A practical walkthrough for a SkyWatcher polar scope on a Celestron Advanced VX — from one-time setup to using it under a dark sky.

s1.title: What polar alignment does
s1.body: Your mount's RA axis must point at the celestial pole so a single motor can track the sky. The polar scope lets you sight the pole star and place it precisely.
tips: The pole is near — but not exactly at — the pole star.
Good alignment = long, round-star exposures and reliable go-to.

s2.title: One-time: collimate the polar scope to the RA axis
s2.body: Center a distant object on the reticle, rotate the RA axis 180°, and adjust the three grub screws to remove half the drift. Repeat until the object stays put as you rotate.
tips: Do this once in daylight on a far landmark (or on Polaris at night).
Adjust the reticle grub screws, never the mount's alt/az bolts.
Tiny turns — the screws are sensitive.

s3.title: Set up the mount (Advanced VX)
s3.body: Level the tripod, set the latitude scale to your latitude, and aim the mount at TRUE north (or south), not magnetic north.
tips: Use a bubble level; an unlevel tripod throws off the latitude setting.
Correct for magnetic declination between compass north and true north.
Pre-set the latitude bolt near your site latitude before you start.

s4.title: See the reticle at night
s4.body: At night you see stars but not the engraved reticle. Illuminate it dimly: shine a RED light obliquely into the front (objective) end, or use the mount's illuminator if fitted.
tips: Red only — white light ruins your dark adaption.
A red phone screen held near the objective works in a pinch.
Keep it dim; too bright washes out faint Polaris.

s5.title: Place the pole star
s5.body: Rotate the RA axis until the reticle's pole-star marker is at the clock position shown above, then use the mount's ALT and AZ bolts (not RA) to move the star into the marker.
tips: Match the on-screen orientation (inverting/erect) to your scope.
Move with the slow alt/az bolts; leave RA where you set it.
Center the star in the small circle, not on the true-pole cross.

s6.title: Verify and refine
s6.body: Cross-check with the Advanced VX hand controller's All-Star Polar Align, or do a quick drift check on a star near the meridian and tweak the alt/az bolts.
tips: All-Star uses any bright star — handy when Polaris is hidden.
Re-check after the mount settles or if you bump the tripod.

scene.title: The system, in three dimensions
scene.body: Every planet is where it actually is right now, tilted on its real axis and turned to its real rotation angle. Drag to orbit, shift-drag to pan, scroll to zoom — and keep zooming: the view runs continuously from outside Neptune's orbit down to a moon a few hundred kilometres across.

time.title: Running the machine
time.body: The scrubber spans 1800 to 2050, the years the orbital model is fitted for. Set a speed — from real time up to a century a second — and run it in either direction. Now snaps back to this instant.

scale.title: Honest, or legible
scale.body: At true scale the inner planets are a knot at the centre and Neptune is off the screen. The distance control compresses the radial field so the whole system reads at once, and the body-size control inflates the worlds themselves. Neither touches the arithmetic: the numbers beside the picture stay true.

bodies.title: Picking a world
bodies.body: Click a body, a label, or a name in the list, and the camera flies to it and follows. The panel then gives its size, mass, rotation, axial tilt, distance from the Sun and from Earth, apparent magnitude and size, phase, and where it is in your sky right now.

legend.title: What is measured and what is modelled
legend.body: Radii, masses and pole directions are published measurements. Each body also carries a chip saying how well its position is known — a fitted orbit is arcminute-class, mean elements are a fraction of a degree. The sources are listed underneath.

targets.title: What is worth shooting tonight
targets.body: The list ranks deep-sky objects for your site and this night: how high each one climbs, how long it stays there, how close the Moon comes to it, and how bright your sky is. The top of the list is simply what you have the best chance of photographing well.

score.title: Why an object scored what it did
score.body: Every score breaks down into its parts, so you can disagree with it. A galaxy that peaks at 25° is a hard target no matter how clear the night is, and a full Moon 20° away costs more than a thin layer of cloud.

skymap.title: The sky map
skymap.body: Selecting a target rings it on the map, so you can see where it will actually be — behind your neighbour's roof, or nicely placed in the south. Object types, sizes and common names come from the OpenNGC catalogue.

weather.title: Astronomy weather
weather.body: Cloud, seeing, transparency, humidity and wind for the coming nights, from several forecast models. Seeing is derived from wind shear rather than taken from a generic index, which tracks reality noticeably better.

darksky.title: Finding a darker site
darksky.body: Pick a night and the finder ranks spots around you, trading darkness against how clear that particular night will be there. It also scores the tree horizon and the real driving distance by road — a perfect dark site three hours away is not a dark site.

optics.title: Your optics
optics.body: Focal length, reducer, barlow and eyepieces feed the field-of-view figures and the framing preview, so the plan matches the equipment you will actually take outside.

why.title: What this page is for
why.body: A GoTo mount only points accurately after it knows where it is. This page picks the alignment stars for you and shows exactly what your hand controller expects, in its own order.

catalogue.title: Your hand controller's own stars
catalogue.body: Celestron and SynScan controllers each carry their own alignment-star list, and they do not agree. Choose yours and the page only ever offers stars that controller can actually be told to use.

sequence.title: The alignment sequence
sequence.body: Stars are chosen to be visible now, well separated across the sky, and bright enough to find in a finder. A two-phase Celestron alignment (align, then calibrate) is laid out step by step.

chart.title: Finding the star
chart.body: Open the chart to see where the star sits relative to its constellation — the part that is genuinely hard when the name means nothing to you yet.

months.title: What is coming
months.body: Eclipses, occultations, conjunctions, meteor showers, comets and ISS passes, computed locally for your site rather than fetched from a feed — so it works offline and stays correct for where you are.

kinds.title: Filtering by kind
kinds.body: Most nights hold something. Filter to the kinds you would actually get out of bed for, then read the rest at leisure.

event.title: One event in full
event.body: Times in your own timezone, altitude at the moment it happens, and how favourable it is from your site. An eclipse that peaks below the horizon is still listed — with that stated plainly.

devices.title: Connecting your gear
devices.body: Camera, filter wheel and mount connect here. A full simulator is always available, so you can learn the whole page indoors before any hardware is plugged in. On an Apple-Silicon Mac a real ZWO camera needs the x86 device server (`just device-x86`) — ZWO publish no arm64 library.

liveview.title: The live view
liveview.body: A continuously refreshed frame with a histogram, a viewfinder and zoom. This is where you confirm the target is framed and the exposure is sane before committing to a sequence.

camera.title: Camera control
camera.body: Exposure, gain, offset, cooling, USB bandwidth — everything the camera reports it can do. Values are written into the FITS header of every frame, which is what lets the stacker match calibration masters later.

filters.title: Filter wheel slots
filters.body: Name each physical slot for the filter currently in it. This mapping is yours to set because a five-slot wheel gets swapped between sessions, and the slot number alone means nothing to the stacker.

sequencer.title: The auto-run sequencer
sequencer.body: Build a plan — so many subs of this filter at this exposure, then the next — and let it run the night. Frames land in per-filter folders with the filter in the filename and the header.

focus.title: Focusing
focus.body: The focus meter measures star size (half-flux diameter) frame by frame. Turn the focuser until the number stops falling; that is a far more reliable signal than judging sharpness by eye.

polar.title: Polar alignment from the camera
polar.body: Measures where your mount's polar axis really points by plate-solving frames as you turn the RA axis BY HAND between them. Turning it yourself is what makes this work on a mount with no electronics at all. It never commands the mount.

list.title: Every night you have shot
list.body: One row per session: what you shot, for how long, through which filters, and how good the sky was. This is what a later stacking decision is actually made from.

score.title: The sky score
score.body: A single 0–100 figure per night, which is the median of the hourly weather verdicts already computed at capture time. Sessions captured before this shipped show 'not recorded' — the weather it needed has no archive, so it can never be filled in afterwards.

filters.title: Finding a session again
filters.body: Filter by object and date to answer 'how much total time do I have on this target, and how much of it is any good?' before deciding whether to shoot it again.

shot.title: What was shot
shot.body: Frame counts and integration per filter and frame type, with the exposure, gain and sensor-temperature ranges. A range collapses to one value when nothing changed mid-run.

order.title: Capture order
order.body: One band per filter across the night, a mark per sub. Lined up with the conditions chart below, this answers 'did the luminance set finish before the cloud arrived, or is half of it from the bad hour?'

conditions.title: The sky that night
conditions.body: Cloud, seeing, transparency, humidity, wind, Moon distance, target altitude and sky brightness, hour by hour. Toggle the overlay to compare the forecast made at the start against what was then measured.

plan.title: Planning a mosaic
plan.body: Give the object and how much sky you want to cover, and the planner lays out overlapping panels for your field of view — with enough overlap for the panels to be matched and blended later.

panels.title: The panels
panels.body: Each panel is a pointing to capture. The plan records where each one goes, so the stacker can reproject them all onto one canvas afterwards instead of guessing from the images alone.

progress.title: Working through them
progress.body: Panels are ticked off as they are captured, across as many nights as it takes. Stack the mosaic once enough panels are done — missing ones simply leave the canvas smaller.

browse.title: Point it at your captures
browse.body: Browse the capture directory (plus removable drives and S3 mirrors) and select one or more folders. Several nights of the same target can be selected together — they will be merged into one run.

inspect.title: What is in there
inspect.body: Inspect reads every file and works out what it is: lights per filter, darks, flats, bias. It uses the FITS headers first, then filenames and folder names, then the pixels themselves. One-shot-colour captures — a DSLR raw or a colour camera — are detected here and stacked as a single RGB channel.

mapping.title: Correcting the channel mapping
mapping.body: When a capture carries no filter names, they are inferred from the signal, and that inference is shown with its confidence. If it guessed wrong, override it here — nothing downstream will argue.

preset.title: Presets
preset.body: Start from a recipe that suits the subject — faint galaxy, star cluster, emission nebula, narrowband palette, moon, planet, comet. A preset only prefills the form; every value stays editable, and you can save your own.

mode.title: Mode and output
mode.body: The mode decides the whole recipe: deepsky, nebula, milkyway, planetary, comet, mosaic or sun. Output is an image, a video, or both.

options.title: The knobs
options.body: Colour calibration, denoise, narrowband handling, palette, stacking algorithm and the per-mode advanced parameters. Every one of them is recorded with the run, so you can always see what produced a given image.

reuse.title: Earlier nights on the same target
reuse.body: Previous sessions of the same object are found automatically and folded in, each one calibrated with its own masters. Deselect any you do not want.

launch.title: Launching
launch.body: Run pipeline starts immediately; Add to queue appends to a strictly sequential lane. Either way it becomes a job you can watch, pause and resume on the Tasks page.

source.title: What to watch
source.body: Point it at the folder your capture software is writing into — or an S3 prefix. It picks up each new sub as it lands.

start.title: Starting
start.body: Frames are calibrated and added to the stack as they arrive, so you see the image deepen through the night instead of waiting until morning to find out it did not work.

preview.title: The growing stack
preview.body: The preview is a real stack, not a single frame — enough to judge framing, focus and whether the target is showing at all.

finalize.title: Stop & finalize
finalize.body: Stopping runs the full pipeline over everything collected: proper registration, grading, stacking and the complete finish. The live preview was the rehearsal; this is the result.

list.title: Everything you have run
list.body: Running jobs and the full history, newest first, with the parameters each was launched with.

status.title: What the states mean
status.body: Running, paused, done, failed or cancelled. Paused is a real checkpoint — a job parked mid-stack keeps its finished channels and resumes from there rather than starting again.

open.title: Opening a job
open.body: Open any job to follow it live, or to read the full result long after it finished.

progress.title: Following a run
progress.body: Live progress over a streaming connection: the current step, the CPU and memory of the tool actually running, and a rolling log. Stacking is long — this is how you tell 'working hard' from 'stuck'.

controls.title: Pause and cancel
controls.body: Pause parks a resumable checkpoint. Cancel stops the run, and a cancel during finishing keeps whatever partial result exists rather than throwing the night away.

previews.title: Previews as it goes
previews.body: A preview is saved after each major milestone, so you can see the stack, the aligned channels and the finish appear rather than waiting for a single image at the end.

results.title: Reading the result
results.body: Per-channel statistics (frames in, frames stacked, which masters matched), per-frame quality charts, warnings, and the full list of parameters used. If a run disappointed you, the reason is almost always here.

stages.title: Changing your mind
stages.body: Each milestone is a card whose parameters you can edit and re-run from — usually far cheaper than starting over. Refine re-runs only the finish; the 3D view opens the field as a volume for any run that plate-solved.

gallery.title: Results on disk
gallery.body: Every run found on disk, independent of the database — anything with a run.json is here. Results survive a database reset.

open.title: Reopening one
open.body: Opening a run rebuilds the same result panels as the job page: final image, per-channel statistics, previews and the parameters that produced it.

masters.title: Your master frames
masters.body: Darks, flats, bias and dark-flats, built once and reused across sessions. This is why a later run does not need you to re-shoot calibration frames.

keys.title: How a master gets matched
keys.body: Masters are keyed by gain, offset, binning, exposure and sensor temperature. A run only uses a master that genuinely matches its lights — a mismatched one is dropped rather than applied.

mirror.title: Keeping a copy on S3
mirror.body: Copy the library to S3 and matched masters are pulled back automatically when they are missing locally — so freeing disk space does not cost you your calibration.

connections.title: Connecting S3
connections.body: Endpoint, access key and secret. The secret is encrypted before it is stored and is never shown again or sent back to the browser.

browse.title: Local and remote side by side
browse.body: Each folder shows whether it exists locally, on S3, or both — so you always know what freeing something would actually cost you.

free.title: Freeing local disk
free.body: Freeing verifies every file is present on S3 BEFORE deleting the local copy, and aborts the whole folder if any check fails. Freed previews and results still open — they fall back to S3 transparently.

backup.title: Backup and restore
backup.body: Backs up the database and browser-side state (favourites, setups, agent chats). Secrets in your .env are deliberately excluded. Restoring the database is destructive — it replaces what is there.

chat.title: A local model over your data
chat.body: Ask about your captures, runs, sky and equipment. The model runs on your own machine — nothing is sent anywhere.

tools.title: It can look things up
tools.body: It can read your inventories and runs, check tonight's sky, and attach an image for a measured critique rather than a vague opinion.

confirm.title: Nothing happens without you
confirm.body: Every action that would change something — launching a run, re-tuning a finish — asks first. Supervised runs also appear here as conversations you can steer while they work.

dither.headline: Dithering moves the TELESCOPE a few pixels between frames. It never touches your images.
dither.notProcessing: Nothing is processed, altered or resampled on the way to disk — every frame is saved exactly as the camera produced it. The only thing that happens is a small nudge of the mount between exposures.
dither.why: Why it helps: hot pixels, dark-current residue and flat-field imperfections sit at FIXED positions on the sensor. Without dithering they land on the same part of the sky in every frame, so stacking averages them in as permanent speckles — and slow tracking drift smears them into ‘walking noise’ streaks. Nudged a few pixels between frames, they fall somewhere new each time and stack rejection removes them entirely.
dither.value: The number is how many frames to take between nudges:
dither.value0: 0 — never dither (use this for darks, bias and flats, and when no mount is connected).
dither.value1: 1 — nudge after every frame: the best noise rejection, the most settle time.
dither.value5: 3 to 5 — the usual choice for long deep-sky subs: nearly all the benefit, a few seconds lost per dither.
dither.valueBig: 10 or more — for short subs where settle time would dominate.
dither.cost: What it costs: about two seconds of settling per nudge, and a slightly smaller area shared by every frame (the offsets are a few pixels, so the loss is negligible).
dither.how: How the offsets are chosen: not randomly. Each nudge is placed as far as possible from every previous one — in whole pixels and in sub-pixel position — and the achieved shift is measured from the next frame, so mount backlash is corrected instead of assumed.
dither.safety: If the mount refuses to move, the dither is skipped with a message and the sequence carries on. A dither can never lose you a frame.
dither.needsMount: Dithering needs a connected mount — it will be skipped until one is connected.
dither.needsScale: Dithering needs the image scale (focal length and pixel size) to convert pixels into a mount movement — it will be skipped.

prepare.camera: Connect the camera and switch the live view on.

prepare.clutch: Be ready to turn the right-ascension axis by hand between frames: release the clutch, or use the hand controller.
prepare.orPole: In a hurry? Set declination to its 90° index so the tube looks straight down the right-ascension axis, point roughly at the pole, and press Find the pole. One frame, no turning.

result.alreadyGood: Nothing to do — the axis is already within an arcminute of the pole.

adjust.instruction: Turn the altitude and azimuth bolts until the ring on the image sits on the centre crosshairs. Do not touch the right-ascension or declination axes.
adjust.offFrame: The marker is off the edge of the frame — keep turning in the direction of the arrow until it comes into view.
adjust.suspect: The field has moved further than the bolts can account for. The mount was probably knocked or slewed; measure again.

stats.precisionHint: One-sigma uncertainty of the measurement, in its worst-constrained direction.

paramDocs.saturation: Overall colour saturation of the final image. Higher is more vivid; too high turns stars garish.
paramDocs.star_desat: Pushes the brightest star cores toward white. Fixes solid colour discs on dense clusters and magenta SHO stars. 0 = off.
paramDocs.lum_opacity: Opacity of the L (luminance) layer in an LRGB composite. 1 = all detail from L; lower is softer and more colour-driven.
paramDocs.ha_screen: Opacity of the red Hα layer screened over the image (only when an Hα channel is present). Higher = stronger red nebulosity.
paramDocs.ha_black_point: Clips the Hα layer's background to black so its red lifts only bright HII knots, not the whole sky.
paramDocs.ha_exclude_stars: Screens Hα onto nebulosity only (stars removed first) so the red doesn't tint stars orange/pink.
paramDocs.ha_continuum_sub: Subtracts the scaled broadband continuum (k·R) from the linear Hα master before stretching, so the red screen shows only true Hα emission: stars and the galaxy disc cancel out and faint filaments survive the black point.
paramDocs.chroma_blur: Blurs colour noise in the LRGB composite (pixels); the L layer keeps all detail. Higher smooths colour and flattens mottle.
paramDocs.core_highlight_knee: Where the nebula-CORE highlight roll-off begins on the luminance. Below it nothing changes — for blown nebula cores, not clusters.
paramDocs.core_highlight_ceil: How far below white a blown nebula core is capped (with core_highlight_knee). Lower = a deeper, more structured core.
paramDocs.highlight_knee: Where the star-safe highlight cap begins on the final image — keeps bright star cores from clipping to white.
paramDocs.highlight_ceil: How far below white bright star cores are capped (with highlight_knee). Lower = cores stay more coloured, less burnt.
paramDocs.crop_frac: Fraction trimmed off each edge to drop the ragged dithered stacking-edge bands.
paramDocs.palette: Colour rendering: gold (Hα), neutral (white light), native (measured from your own recording), mono, or inverted.
paramDocs.color_calibration: Photometric colour calibration (SPCC) for natural star/nebula hues; falls back to a neutral balance when offline.
paramDocs.linked_stretch: Stretches all channels together to preserve the calibrated colour balance (vs per-channel, which re-tints).
paramDocs.background_level: How bright the sky renders. 0 is pure black; around 0.05 gives the warm pedestal most published solar images have.
paramDocs.stretch_headroom: Caps bright star cores this far below white BEFORE the stretch so they keep colour instead of burning. 0 = off; lower = more protection.
paramDocs.background_degree: Degree of the Siril polynomial used to model and subtract the sky background/gradient.
paramDocs.combined_background_ai: A second gradient-extraction pass on the combined RGB — removes the large-scale gradient / brown sky the per-channel pass leaves.
paramDocs.color_denoise_ai: AI colour denoise on the linear RGB — cuts chroma noise without blurring detail (unlike a blur).
paramDocs.chroma_smooth_px: Star-protected colour-only smoothing of the linear RGB (px). Flattens residual colour patches; luminance and star colours are untouched. 0 disables.
paramDocs.chroma_bg_smooth_px: Extra colour smoothing restricted to the sky background (px). Removes large-scale colour mottle; galaxies, nebulae and stars keep their colour. 0 disables.
paramDocs.star_reduce: StarNet++ star-reduction opacity in the finish: 1 = full stars, 0.5 = halved, 0 = keep all.
paramDocs.fwhm_sigma: Frame rejection: drop subs whose star sharpness (FWHM) is worse than this many σ from the session. Lower rejects harder.
paramDocs.roundness_floor: Frame rejection: minimum star roundness to keep a sub — drops trailed / wind-shaken frames. Higher keeps only rounder stars.
paramDocs.background_sigma: Frame rejection: drop subs whose background is this many σ above the median (clouds, moonlight, gradients).
paramDocs.star_count_frac: Frame rejection: keep only subs with at least this fraction of the best sub's detected star count.
paramDocs.trail_mask_k: Cross-frame satellite/plane trail masking: a pixel above the per-pixel median + k·σ is replaced. Lower = more aggressive; 0 = off.
paramDocs.denoise_lum: Denoise strength on the linear LUMINANCE master — gentle, to preserve galaxy/nebula detail.
paramDocs.denoise_chroma: Denoise strength on the linear COLOUR channels — usually higher, since thin R/G/B sub-stacks are noisy.
paramDocs.background_ai: GraXpert AI background/gradient extraction on each linear master (instead of Siril's polynomial subsky).
paramDocs.stretch: Midtone lift. Higher shows more faint surface detail.
paramDocs.highlight: Highlight-protection point — higher keeps bright craters and the limb from clipping to white.
paramDocs.shadow_lift: Opens up the shadows (crater floors, the terminator side) by sliding the stretch's focus point toward black (0–1). 0 = off (the historical curve); higher reveals more dark detail without touching the protected highlights.
paramDocs.sharpen: Wavelet detail boost. 1.0 is default; raise for more crater/band detail, lower if it rings or looks crunchy.
paramDocs.clahe: Local contrast / surface relief. Higher is punchier; too high looks harsh.
paramDocs.headroom: Scales the bright disk down before the stretch so highlights don't burn. 0 or 1 = no scaling; in-between reserves more room.
paramDocs.limb_balance: Compresses the smooth illumination of the bright limb band while keeping local crater contrast intact (0–1) — the burnt-white limb regains its detail without dimming the terminator. 0 = off.
paramDocs.earthshine_gain: Brightness of the revealed earthshine (the Moon's unlit side): 0 = off, 1 = natural (~10% grey), up to 2. Lifts real stacked signal only — skipped with a note when the dark side is below the noise floor or the disc is fully lit.
paramDocs.earthshine_feather: Terminator protection margin of the earthshine blend, as a fraction of the disc radius (0.002–0.02, default 0.006): larger keeps the lift farther from the lit edge — the lit surface itself is never touched at any value.
paramDocs.true_lum: Colour runs re-impose the sharp, deconvolved L as the exact output luminance after the RGB compose (fixes Siril's rgbcomp luminance leak that softens the final image). Default on; disable only if colour artefacts appear.
paramDocs.best_percent: Lucky-imaging frame selection: keep only this % of the sharpest frames before stacking. Lower = stricter.
paramDocs.ap_align: Correct atmospheric distortion with a grid of alignment points instead of one rigid transform. The atmosphere does not displace the disc as a rigid object, so without this the stack averages every feature against slightly shifted copies of itself.
paramDocs.double_stack: Second alignment pass onto the first stacked master (a low-noise, distortion-averaged reference) with a much denser alignment-point grid — AutoStakkert's double-stack reference. Sharper, ~1.7× slower.
paramDocs.calibrate: Applies master dark/flat calibration to the frames (masters built from the capture's own dark/flat/offset folders, or reused from the library). Removes dust shadows, vignetting and colour blotches; skipped automatically when nothing matches.
paramDocs.deconv_fwhm: Deconvolution PSF width (pixels) — set near the blur size to recover detail. 0 = off.
paramDocs.deconv_auto: Measure the deconvolution width from the limb instead of naming it. The limb is a step, so what smears it is the system's own blur — optics, seeing and the camera's processing together. On, the run deconvolves at that measured width and backs off when it detects the camera already sharpened the frames. Setting a width by hand turns this off.
paramDocs.bracket_merge: Stack exposures shot a stop or more apart separately, then composite them into one high-dynamic-range master — disc detail from the exposure that holds it, prominences from the one that recorded them. Off, a bracketed session is normalised onto one level and only its brightest exposure is rendered.
paramDocs.bracket_stops: How far apart two captures' disc brightness must be, in stops, before they count as separate exposures. Below this they are one exposure drifting; above it they are a deliberate bracket.
paramDocs.transparency_floor: Drop frames a cloud passed in front of, below this fraction of the clip's clearest transmission. A cloud is not a sharpness problem: it adds a veil that averaging cannot remove, and normalisation afterwards scales that veil up with the signal so it reaches the stack looking correctly exposed. 0 turns the gate off.
paramDocs.sequence_panels: Render the eclipse progression sheet: this many phases, stepping from a shallow bite through maximum and back out, all brought into one sky frame. 0 renders none. The number is a request, not a promise — which phases exist on BOTH sides of maximum belongs to the recording, so a session with a gap in it gets the most panels it can pair honestly and says how many that was. Nothing is ever mirrored or interpolated.
paramDocs.sequence_angle_deg: The rise of the line the panels sit on, as it is seen: positive climbs to the right, 0 lays them in a row.
paramDocs.sequence_spacing: Centre-to-centre step between panels, in solar diameters, so it means the same thing whatever size the discs end up rendered at. Below 1 the discs overlap.
paramDocs.site_lat: Latitude the capture was made at. Only needed when the clips carry no location tag of their own — a phone writes one, most cameras do not — and an eclipse's phase cannot be computed without it.
paramDocs.site_lon: Longitude the capture was made at, east-positive. See the latitude note.
paramDocs.ap_scale: How much the frame is reduced before the distortion field is measured. 1 measures at full resolution, which is what the field's amplitude requires — after the limb fit only a few pixels are left to measure, so a reduced raster cannot represent the answer and returns noise instead. Larger values are faster and progressively soften the outer disc.
paramDocs.deconv_iters: Deconvolution iterations. More sharpens further and rings at the limb sooner.
paramDocs.deconv_alpha: Deconvolution regularisation — higher suppresses noise/ringing, lower is more aggressive.
paramDocs.drizzle_scale: Super-resolution output grid (1, 1.5 or 2): the stack accumulates hundreds of sub-pixel-dithered frames onto a finer raster, genuinely adding resolution. Default 1.5; costs ×scale² memory/time (re-stack).
paramDocs.align_points: Total number of stacking reference points used to correct atmospheric-wave distortion (AutoStakkert-style). Snapped to an N×N grid, N = √value clamped to 10–48 per axis (100–2304 total). 0 = automatic (~120 px cells, up to 32×32). More points track finer seeing waves but cost CPU (re-stack); the estimator button in the run form suggests a value from your image.
paramDocs.per_frame_starnet: Runs StarNet++ on every frame before the comet stack (denser fields). Slower, but cleaner star removal.
paramDocs.look: Render style: natural (faithful, soft), iphone (warmer, punchier, deeper sky) or deepsky (bold, dramatic, high saturation).
paramDocs.projection: Which sky canvas to draw: stereographic keeps star shapes and renders the sky as you look up at it; galactic lays the Milky Way out as a level band; altaz draws the arch as it stood over the ground at one instant (the middle of the session); both writes the first two, all writes all three.
paramDocs.scale_deg_per_pix: Canvas scale in degrees per pixel. The panels themselves are about 0.02, so going much finer than 0.03 buys pixels rather than detail — a star cannot be placed more precisely than the plate solution's own residual.
paramDocs.group_step_deg: How far consecutive frames may move on the sky before they count as a new pointing. Raise it when a drifting session split one pointing in two; lower it when two real pointings were merged.
paramDocs.band_mask_lat_deg: Galactic latitude inside which canvas pixels count as the Milky Way band rather than background sky. The band is the subject: measuring the sky's own level and colour inside it would neutralise the Milky Way to grey.
paramDocs.pano_background: Remove the residual sky dome from the assembled canvas with a low-order polynomial fitted outside the band. Off keeps the canvas photometrically raw.
paramDocs.pano_foreground: Composite the landscape under the arch, taken from whichever panel was aimed lowest — the only one with any ground in it. Applies to the altaz canvas only: the other projections have no horizon to stand it on. The ground is placed by turning that panel's camera about the celestial pole by the time between when it was shot and the instant the arch is drawn for.
paramDocs.keep_meteors: Blend the meteors the sigma-clip rejected back into the sky, and leave the satellites and aircraft out. The clip is right that a meteor is an outlier and wrong only to discard it. Every candidate is recorded in meteors.json with the reason it was kept or dropped. Off keeps the run identical to one built without it.
paramDocs.brightness: Target sky-background level. Lower = a darker sky; higher lifts the Milky-Way core.
paramDocs.saturation_scale: Scales the chosen look's own saturation. 1 = as designed; below 1 tames neon colour; up to 2 for more.
paramDocs.highlight_ceiling: The Milky-Way core's brightness ceiling. Lower = a dimmer, better-protected core; 0 keeps the look's own.
paramDocs.seam_offset_refit: Re-measures each night's sky pedestal inside its overlap with the anchor night and corrects it before stacking — removes the straight background steps at the rotated footprint boundaries of multi-night masters.
paramDocs.seam_noise_eq: Fades the grain change where fewer nights cover the sky: a coverage-weighted denoise that is exactly zero in the full-depth core and ramps up in single-night zones — the noise part of the seam cut-lines.
paramDocs.mosaic: Keeps the union of every night's field (bigger canvas, no pixel lost) instead of cropping to the anchor night's frame. Consent knob: reruns never re-enable it on their own.
paramDocs.mosaic_fill: What happens to mosaic regions no session ever covered: crop trims the final to the field where every channel has data (default); fill keeps the whole union with extrapolated sky + matched grain.
paramDocs.oiii_screen: Opacity of the teal [OIII] layer screened over the image (only when OIII was captured beside a real B filter). 0 = off; raise it to make shock fronts glow blue-green beside the red Hα.
paramDocs.oiii_black_point: Clips the [OIII] layer's background to black before it is screened, so the teal lifts only real emission and never the sky noise.
paramDocs.sii_screen: Opacity of the [SII] layer screened over the image (only when SII was captured). 0 = off; raise it to bring sulphur structure out beside the red Hα and the teal [OIII].
paramDocs.sii_black_point: Clips the [SII] layer's background to black before it is screened, so its tint lifts only real emission and never the sky noise.
paramDocs.sii_tint: Colour of the [SII] screen. [SII] at 672 nm is DEEPER red than Hα, which a screen cannot show — so pick how to tell them apart. Deep red is a crimson that reads as natural; gold is the amber accent the Hubble palette established, and is far easier to see against the Hα layer.
paramDocs.sky_chroma_flatten_px: Neutralizes the sky's large-scale colour AFTER the stretch (grid px). The stretch amplifies sub-percent background colour residuals into visible left-right bands or coloured discs; this measures the sky colour per tile and subtracts it — sky turns neutral, objects keep their colour. 0 disables.
paramDocs.sky_lum_flatten_px: Equalizes the sky's large-scale brightness AFTER the stretch (px of grid). Fits a smooth surface to the sky level and brings the whole sky to one uniform level (the glow-free dark sky) — residual glow comes down, a beyond-glow corner comes up; objects keep their contrast. 0 disables (default for nebula, protecting faint emission wings).
paramDocs.lum_boost: Gently lifts the luminance midtones (value = peak lift at mid-grey; sky level, black point, bright cores and colours pinned) — a brighter galaxy periphery and arms without touching the sky, stars or core detail. 0 disables.
paramDocs.emit_luminance_mono: Also saves a processed monochrome image of just the L channel (final_luminance) next to the colour final — the same calibrated, background-extracted, stretched treatment L gets inside the composite.
paramDocs.emit_all_channel_mono: Also saves one monochrome image integrating every channel (L/R/G/B/Hα…) into a synthetic luminance weighted by sub-count (final_monostack) — the maximum-signal mono view.
paramDocs.union_canvas: Multi-night union canvas (same pointing): keeps the union of every night's field (bigger canvas, no pixel lost) instead of cropping to the anchor night's frame. Consent knob: reruns never re-enable it on their own. Unrelated to the tiled-panel mosaic mode.
paramDocs.union_canvas_fill: What happens to union-canvas regions no session ever covered: crop trims the final to the field where every channel has data (default); fill keeps the whole union with extrapolated sky + matched grain.
paramDocs.overlap_expected: The capture overlap fraction between neighboring panels the plan promised. Scales the blend feather and the panel-detection sanity checks.
paramDocs.feather_frac: Width of the center-weighted blend ramp, as a fraction of the overlap. Wider = smoother seams; each star stays dominated by the panel that sees it nearest its optical axis.
paramDocs.photom_match: How panel photometry is matched on the canvas: gain_offset corrects sky pedestal AND transparency per panel (default), offset corrects pedestal only, off disables matching.
paramDocs.canvas_crop: Edges of the assembled canvas: common crops to the largest rectangle every channel covers (default), union keeps everything, plan crops to the plan's grid bounding box.
paramDocs.min_panel_frames: Panels whose channels stacked fewer total frames are dropped — a stray mis-filed pointing must not become a hole-riddled pseudo-panel.
paramDocs.panel_source: How frames are split into panels: auto tries p01/-style folders then pointing-header clustering, folders and coords force one method.
paramDocs.flat_strength: Removes the etalon's Newton's rings, dust and sweet-spot gradient. 0 leaves the frame alone.
paramDocs.deconv_sigma: Gaussian PSF width, in pixels, used for deconvolution. 0 turns deconvolution off.
paramDocs.sharpen_small: Fine-scale contrast (granulation, filament edges). Above ~1.5 it mostly amplifies noise.
paramDocs.sharpen_medium: Mid-scale contrast (filaments, plage) — the main detail control.
paramDocs.sharpen_large: Large-scale contrast (active regions). Leave near 1 unless the disc looks flat.
paramDocs.sharpen_denoise: Suppresses noise at the finest scales before the gains are applied.
paramDocs.limb_flatten: Removes limb darkening so detail reads all the way to the edge. 0 keeps the natural falloff.
paramDocs.prominence_boost: Brightness of the off-limb prominences relative to the disc. 0 hides them.
paramDocs.prominence_feather: How softly the disc and off-limb renderings blend across the limb, as a fraction of the radius.
paramDocs.background_tint: How much of the palette's own colour the sky carries: 0 neutral grey, 1 full amber.
paramDocs.glow_strength: Brightness of the halo around the disc, as a fraction of what the limb itself renders at. 0 turns it off.
paramDocs.glow_radius: How far that halo reaches beyond the limb, as a fraction of the disc radius.
paramDocs.contrast: Overall contrast of the finished image.
paramDocs.band: Which channel carries the signal: auto-detected, Hα (red only) or white light (all channels).
paramDocs.keep_percent: Percentage of the sharpest frames kept from each source.
paramDocs.max_frames: Hard cap on frames taken from one clip or still set.
paramDocs.drizzle: Stacks onto a finer grid (1, 1.5 or 2). Only helps when the capture is undersampled.
paramDocs.clip_sigma: How far a frame may differ from the stack before that pixel is rejected.
paramDocs.window_seconds: Longest time span in one stack. Shorter keeps the chromosphere frozen and field rotation small.
paramDocs.min_frames: Fewest frames a window needs to be stacked at all; shorter windows are dropped.
paramDocs.crop_margin: How far past the limb the crop reaches, as a fraction of the radius — room for prominences.
paramDocs.scale_tolerance: How closely two files' measured disc sizes must agree to be stacked together.
paramDocs.stack_engine: Which engine combines the pixels: automatic (Siril, unless the chosen algorithm is Go-only), siril, or native (the Go combiner).
paramDocs.stack_combine: How each pixel's surviving samples become one value: mean (optimal), median (robust), sum, max or min.
paramDocs.stack_reject: The outlier test applied before averaging. "auto" adapts to the frame count: percentile ≤7, winsorized 8–49, GESD ≥50.
paramDocs.stack_reject_low: The rejection algorithm's LOW parameter — a σ multiplier, a kept fraction, or GESD's outlier fraction, depending on the algorithm. 0 = its own default.
paramDocs.stack_reject_high: The rejection algorithm's HIGH parameter, in the same units as the low one. 0 = its own default.
paramDocs.stack_trim_frac: Fraction discarded at EACH end by the trimmed mean. Go engine only.
paramDocs.stack_norm: How frames are brought onto one photometric footing: addscale (default), add, mul, mulscale, or none.
paramDocs.stack_fast_norm: Use faster location/scale estimators than the default IKSS. Slightly less robust.
paramDocs.stack_weight: How much each frame counts in the average: none, noise, wfwhm (default), nbstars or nbstack.
paramDocs.stack_rejection_maps: Also write low/high rejection maps — a diagnostic image of where pixels were dropped.
paramDocs.stack_feather: Blend each frame's borders over this many pixels, hiding the hard dithered edges of a drifting sequence. 0 = off.
paramDocs.stack_local_norm: Fit a per-frame polynomial background/transparency surface before rejection (local normalization). Go engine only.
paramDocs.stack_local_norm_degree: Polynomial degree of that local-normalization surface, 1–4. 0 = the engine default.
paramDocs.comet_stack_reject: The rejection used for the COMET-aligned stack of a comet run (the star-aligned half uses stack_reject).
paramDocs.comet_stack_low: σ low for the comet-aligned stack. Loose by default (4) so the faint tail's noisy samples survive.
paramDocs.comet_stack_high: σ high for the comet-aligned stack. Tight by default (1.8) so the marching star trails are erased.
paramDocs.master_bias_combine: Combination method for the bias/offset master — the sensor read-out pedestal; stacked un-normalized because that pedestal IS the signal.
paramDocs.master_bias_reject: Pixel rejection for the bias/offset master. "auto" adapts to THAT pool's own depth, which is usually very different from the light count.
paramDocs.master_bias_low: The bias/offset master's rejection LOW parameter, in its algorithm's own units. 0 = the algorithm's default.
paramDocs.master_bias_high: The bias/offset master's rejection HIGH parameter, same units as the low one. 0 = the algorithm's default.
paramDocs.master_dark_combine: Combination method for the dark master — thermal signal and hot pixels; stacked un-normalized, and the rejection decides which flickering (RTS) pixels reach the defect map.
paramDocs.master_dark_reject: Pixel rejection for the dark master. "auto" adapts to THAT pool's own depth, which is usually very different from the light count.
paramDocs.master_dark_low: The dark master's rejection LOW parameter, in its algorithm's own units. 0 = the algorithm's default.
paramDocs.master_dark_high: The dark master's rejection HIGH parameter, same units as the low one. 0 = the algorithm's default.
paramDocs.master_flat_combine: Combination method for the flat master — vignetting and dust; stacked multiplicatively because only the relative shape matters.
paramDocs.master_flat_reject: Pixel rejection for the flat master. "auto" adapts to THAT pool's own depth, which is usually very different from the light count.
paramDocs.master_flat_low: The flat master's rejection LOW parameter, in its algorithm's own units. 0 = the algorithm's default.
paramDocs.master_flat_high: The flat master's rejection HIGH parameter, same units as the low one. 0 = the algorithm's default.
paramDocs.master_dark_flat_combine: Combination method for the dark-flat master — the flats' own dark; it calibrates the flats, so it stacks like a dark.
paramDocs.master_dark_flat_reject: Pixel rejection for the dark-flat master. "auto" adapts to THAT pool's own depth, which is usually very different from the light count.
paramDocs.master_dark_flat_low: The dark-flat master's rejection LOW parameter, in its algorithm's own units. 0 = the algorithm's default.
paramDocs.master_dark_flat_high: The dark-flat master's rejection HIGH parameter, same units as the low one. 0 = the algorithm's default.

STANDARD.label: Standard
STANDARD.blurb: The classic hot tier — instant access, no retrieval fee. The destination when restoring cold data.

GLACIER_IR.label: Glacier Instant Retrieval
GLACIER_IR.blurb: Cheap archival storage but still instant reads (no thaw). Good for masters/results you re-read occasionally.

GLACIER.label: Glacier Flexible Retrieval
GLACIER.blurb: Low-cost archive; objects must be restored (minutes–hours) before download. The main “archive it” target.

DEEP_ARCHIVE.label: Deep Archive
DEEP_ARCHIVE.blurb: Cheapest, coldest tier; restore can take up to ~48h. For long-term backups you rarely touch.

stacking.sectionHint: How the frames are combined into one master, and which pixels are thrown away first.
stacking.autoChose: Your deepest channel has {n} frames, so the engine picks this on its own. Choose an algorithm explicitly to override it.
stacking.noRejection: This method combines every sample, so no outlier test applies.
stacking.cometRejectHint: The comet half of the run is clipped asymmetrically by default: the coma sits still while the stars march through it, so the high side is tight and the low side loose. Leave it on automatic unless star trails survive.
stacking.fastNormHint: Quicker, very slightly less robust than the default IKSS.
stacking.rejectionMapsHint: An extra diagnostic image showing where pixels were dropped.
stacking.engineOverride: Stacking is pinned to the {engine} engine for this run.
stacking.trimFracHint: Discarded at EACH end before averaging. 0.1 drops the highest and lowest 10 %.
stacking.localNormHint: Fits a background/transparency surface per frame before rejection. Go engine only.
stacking.featherHint: Blends each frame's borders over this many pixels, hiding the hard edges of a drifting sequence. 0 = off.
stacking.mastersHint: Each frame type is stacked separately, and their pools differ by an order of magnitude — 200 bias frames and 5 flats want opposite algorithms — so each carries its own recipe.
stacking.mastersVariantNote: A non-default recipe builds its master under its own filename, so it can never overwrite the shared library master your other runs depend on.

frameTypeHint.master_bias: The sensor's read-out pedestal. Usually the deepest pool you have, so GESD often beats the default — and it is stacked un-normalized, because that pedestal IS the signal.
frameTypeHint.master_dark: Thermal signal and hot pixels. Also un-normalized. Rejection here decides which flickering (RTS) pixels end up in the defect map.
frameTypeHint.master_flat: Vignetting and dust. Stacked multiplicatively — only the relative shape matters. Flat sets are usually small, so a gentle test beats an aggressive one.
frameTypeHint.master_dark_flat: The flats' own dark. It calibrates the flats, so it stacks like a dark.

mean.label: Average (with rejection)
mean.desc: Adds the frames and divides. With Gaussian noise this is the mathematically optimal combination — nothing else extracts more signal-to-noise from the same subs.
mean.expect: The deepest, smoothest result. This is the right default for essentially every deep-sky stack.

median.label: Median
median.desc: Takes the middle value of each pixel. Immune to outliers without any tuning, but it throws away information: the noise only falls as if you had about 64% of your frames.
median.expect: A visibly noisier master than the average for the same subs. Worth it only for a handful of very dissimilar frames, or as a sanity check.

sum.label: Sum
sum.desc: Pure addition, with no rejection and no normalization. Keeps every photon and the original linear scale.
sum.expect: Maximum faint signal, but every satellite trail, cosmic ray and plane stays in the image. Mostly useful for very short planetary or ultra-faint sequences.

max.label: Maximum
max.desc: Keeps the brightest sample of each pixel across the sequence.
max.expect: Not a noise-reduction tool: it builds star-trail and meteor composites, where you WANT every transient kept.

min.label: Minimum
min.desc: Keeps the darkest sample of each pixel.
min.expect: A diagnostic rather than a picture — it shows what is present in every single frame, which makes it good for spotting a persistent artefact.

trimmed_mean.label: Trimmed mean
trimmed_mean.desc: Sorts each pixel's samples, discards a fixed fraction at both ends, and averages what remains. A blunt but completely predictable robust average.
trimmed_mean.expect: Close to the average's depth with the median's tolerance for outliers. Useful when the noise is not Gaussian and a sigma-based test misbehaves.

none.label: No rejection
none.desc: Every sample is kept. Nothing is tested and nothing is discarded.
none.expect: Maximum signal and maximum contamination: any trail, cosmic ray or aircraft in a single sub survives into the master.

percentile.label: Percentile clipping
percentile.desc: Drops a fixed fraction of the highest and lowest samples instead of measuring a spread. On a handful of frames a measured sigma is meaningless, so this is the only honest test available.
percentile.expect: Reliable cleaning of small stacks. On a deep stack it wastes good data — it always drops the same share, however clean the pixel is.

sigma.label: Sigma clipping (kappa-sigma)
sigma.desc: Iteratively measures each pixel's mean and spread and drops the samples further than κ·σ from it. The classic, well-understood outlier test.
sigma.expect: Solid general cleaning. A very bright outlier inflates the sigma it is measured against, so a few strong trail pixels can slip through — that is what Winsorized clipping fixes.

median_sigma.label: Median sigma clipping
median_sigma.desc: Sigma clipping centred on the median instead of the mean, so the outliers being hunted do not drag the centre toward themselves.
median_sigma.expect: Slightly more robust than plain sigma clipping on asymmetric contamination, at essentially no cost.

winsorized.label: Winsorized sigma clipping
winsorized.desc: Before measuring the spread, extreme samples are pulled in to the edge of the distribution (Huber winsorization) rather than deleted. The sigma is then estimated from data the outliers cannot inflate.
winsorized.expect: The best all-round compromise, and the reason it is the default for 8–50 frames: it removes trails and cosmic rays without eating faint real signal.

linear_fit.label: Linear fit clipping
linear_fit.desc: Fits a robust straight line through each pixel's samples and rejects the ones that fall off it, so a smoothly CHANGING level is modelled instead of being treated as noise.
linear_fit.expect: The right choice when the sky itself moved during the session — a rising moon, drifting light pollution, a gradient that walks across the frame. On a stable sky it is no better than Winsorized.

gesd.label: GESD (extreme studentized deviate)
gesd.desc: A formal statistical test that repeatedly asks whether the most extreme remaining sample is a genuine outlier, up to a maximum fraction, at a chosen significance level.
gesd.expect: The most rigorous option on large stacks, and the reason it is the default past 50 frames: it catches the correlated leftovers — walking noise, faint trail remnants — that a fixed 3σ clip leaves behind.

mad.label: MAD clipping
mad.desc: Clips at k times the median absolute deviation, a spread estimate that ignores the outliers entirely rather than being computed from them.
mad.expect: Very robust on ugly data. It is a blunter instrument than Winsorized clipping — expect it to reject a little more than strictly necessary.

rcr.label: Robust Chauvenet rejection
rcr.desc: Applies Chauvenet's criterion with robust statistics, deciding how many samples a stack of this size should contain by chance rather than using a fixed threshold.
rcr.expect: Adapts its aggressiveness to the stack depth on its own. Strong on heavily contaminated data; runs in the Go engine, so it is slower than Siril's own tests.

adaptive_weighted.label: Auto-adaptive weighted average
adaptive_weighted.desc: Instead of a hard keep-or-drop decision, it iterates a weight per sample until the weights converge, so a marginal sample fades out rather than disappearing at a threshold.
adaptive_weighted.expect: Smoother than a hard clip, with no threshold artefacts — DeepSkyStacker's signature mode. Runs in the Go engine and costs several passes over the data.

entropy_weighted.label: Entropy-weighted average
entropy_weighted.desc: Weights each frame's contribution by the local information content around the pixel, favouring the frames that actually resolve detail there.
entropy_weighted.expect: Can preserve fine structure better than a plain average on variable seeing. Runs in the Go engine, and it is a look as much as a noise tool — compare before committing.

none.label: None
none.desc: Frames are combined exactly as they are. Correct for calibration masters, where the pedestal IS the signal.

add.label: Additive
add.desc: Levels the sky background between frames by an offset only. Use when transparency held steady and only the sky level drifted.

addscale.label: Additive + scaling
addscale.desc: Levels both the background AND the contrast between frames. The deep-sky default: it lets subs shot through different transparency stack together fairly.

mul.label: Multiplicative
mul.desc: Scales frames by a ratio rather than shifting them. The physically correct choice for flat fields, where only the relative shape matters.

mulscale.label: Multiplicative + scaling
mulscale.desc: Multiplicative levelling with a spread correction as well. Rarely needed on lights.

none.label: Equal weight
none.desc: Every frame counts the same, however good or bad it is.

noise.label: By noise
noise.desc: The quietest frames count most. The best purely statistical choice when depth matters more than sharpness.

wfwhm.label: By sharpness (wFWHM)
wfwhm.desc: The sharpest frames count most, measured by star width weighted by star count. The default: it keeps a soft sub from blurring the master.

nbstars.label: By star count
nbstars.desc: Frames that detected more stars count most — a good proxy for transparency, so thin cloud is demoted.

nbstack.label: By sub-count
nbstack.desc: For stacking already-stacked images: each input counts in proportion to how many subs went into it.
